desc:
The min-product of a non-empty subarray is the minimum value of the subarray multiplied by the sum of the subarray. Find the largest min-product over all non-empty subarrays of nums and return it modulo 1,000,000,007. The maximum must be chosen by its true value, before taking the remainder.

Example: for [1, 2, 3, 2] the best subarray is [2, 3, 2] with minimum 2 and sum 7, giving 14.
constraints: The true maximum can exceed 32 bits; only its remainder modulo 1,000,000,007 is returned
hints: For a fixed minimum value, which subarray is the best? All values are positive, so a longer subarray has a larger sum.
Assume nums[i] is the minimum. Extend the subarray left and right as far as every element stays ≥ nums[i]. That subarray has the best sum among those with minimum at least nums[i] around i.

Use prefix sums for the sum and a monotonic stack of increasing values to find the extent: when an element pops a taller bar, the popped element's range ends just before the current index and starts after the new stack top. Append a sentinel 0 so everything is popped at the end.
editorial: Because every value is positive, enlarging a subarray without lowering its minimum only increases the sum. So the optimal subarray is the maximal one around some index i in which nums[i] is the minimum, namely the span from just after the nearest smaller element on the left to just before the nearest smaller element on the right. There are only n such spans.

Build prefix sums pre. Scan the array with a stack of indices whose values are non-decreasing. When the current value is smaller than the value on top, pop that index m: its span ends at cur - 1 and starts at stack[-1] + 1 (or 0 when the stack is empty). The candidate is nums[m] * (pre[cur] - pre[start]). A final sentinel value 0 flushes the stack. Keep the maximum as an exact integer and reduce modulo 109+7 only at the end, because taking remainders earlier would break the comparison. Time O(n).
